One primary concept each, checked for duplicated required answers as well as duplicated labels. Q1 the whole Book 8 specimen anchor, speciation then the direct-indirect split then three LO (d) mechanisms then a ranking judgement · Q2 sequestration as named biomolecules, then arithmetic, then a judgement against your own number · Q3 CO2e computed across five gases, potency held apart from total contribution · Q4 the carbon cycle end to end and why a large sink still leaves a net rise · Q5 sink and source defined by net direction, and what flips one into the other · Q6 the properties that separate CO2 from methane, and a rate-of-change axis · Q7 the land and food side of the footprint · Q8 proxies, and describing a record with quoted data · Q9 the discuss archetype at full length.

The three deliberately shared marking points, declared. First, greenhouse gases absorb longwave or infrared radiation and re-emit it, trapping heat in the atmosphere, which a prelim scheme in this Book makes a compulsory point even inside a question about human activities; it is required in Q4, Q5(c) and Q6(c) and that repetition is the point. Second, deforestation removes a carbon sink, which Q1(b) needs as its whole answer and Q7(a) needs as one of two routes from meat production to CO2; the two are not interchangeable, because Q1(b) is marked on the word indirect and Q7(a) is marked on land conversion. Third, crop plants absorb CO2 as they grow, offsetting what is released on combustion, which Q1(d) needs alone and Q9 needs as one of twelve possible marks. Every other required answer in the set is unique.

Nothing from Book 9, and nothing from chapter 8.1 beyond the greenhouse mechanism. Roughly 12% of chapter 8.1 is examinable, 26 pages carrying about 3. Albedo, biomes, El Nino, orbital cycles and volcanic aerosols are out; LO (a) is explicit that the outcome is anthropogenic. Nitrous oxide appears only where a paper printed it, because LO (a) says limited to CO2 and methane. Mangroves, coral, feedback loops and the effects on organisms are Cluster 2; food supply, biodiversity and dengue are Cluster 3.

Question 1 [16 marks]

Over thousands and millions of years, the Earth's climate is subject to natural periods of warming and cooling. Figure 8.1 is a diagram representing two mountains in the tropics during a warm phase and a cool phase in the Earth's climate. The shape of the lines corresponds to a vertical section through the mountains to show their height and shape. The distribution of rain forest vegetation with altitude is shown by the hatched shading.

(a) Suggest how repeated changes in climate between the warm phase and cool phase shown in Figure 8.1 may lead to the evolution of new species and greater species diversity. [5]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Figure 8.1, suggest how repeated changes in climate between the warm phase and cool phase may lead to the evolution of new species and greater species diversity. [5] [INFERRED: the 9477 specimen ships without a mark scheme. The chain below is Core Idea 4 LO (j) allopatric speciation, cross-checked against the standard prelim keys for geographic-isolation speciation]

1. In the warm phase the rain forest is restricted to a band near the tops of the two mountains, so the two patches of rain forest are separated by unsuitable lowland habitat, and any rain forest population is split into two geographically isolated populations.

2. Gene flow between the two isolated populations stops, because individuals cannot cross the hot lowland between the peaks to interbreed.

3. The two populations experience different selection pressures, and different random mutations arise in each population, so different alleles are selected for in each and allele frequencies diverge.

4. Over many generations the accumulated genetic differences produce reproductive isolation, so that when the cool phase reconnects the forest the two populations can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring, and they are now separate species.

5. Because the warm and cool phases repeat, the cycle of isolation, divergence and reconnection happens again and again, each cycle generating further new species, so species diversity increases over time.

(b) In the last 200 years, the Earth has undergone a new kind of global warming as a result of anthropogenic activities that increase the amount of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. Some of these activities, such as generating electricity, act directly by releasing greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. Others act indirectly to contribute to increases in greenhouse gases in the atmosphere.

State one anthropogenic activity that indirectly contributes to increases in greenhouse gases in the atmosphere and explain how the activity results in these increases. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) State one anthropogenic activity that indirectly contributes to increases in greenhouse gases in the atmosphere and explain how the activity results in these increases. [2] [INFERRED: no official key]

1. Activity: deforestation, meaning the clearance of forest for agriculture, timber or building.

2. Explanation: removing the trees removes a carbon sink, so less carbon dioxide is taken out of the atmosphere by photosynthesis, and the concentration of CO2 in the atmosphere rises even though the deforestation itself did not release it. That last clause is what makes it indirect.

3. Accept alternatives with a matching explanation: cattle farming or rice paddies, because anaerobic bacteria in the rumen or in waterlogged soil release methane; use of nitrogen fertilisers, because denitrifying bacteria convert the nitrate to nitrous oxide; landfill, because anaerobic decomposition of buried organic waste releases methane.

4. A separate prelim scheme on the same distinction rejects enlarging cities and choice of food where a direct cause was asked for, on the grounds that these cause deforestation and so are indirect causes. Here the stem asks for indirect, so read which word the question used.

(c) Table 8.1 shows one measure for assessing the carbon footprint of six different energy sources when used to generate electricity. This measure is calculated over the entire life of the device used to generate electricity and is expressed as the total mass of greenhouse gases (grams of carbon dioxide equivalent) released for each megajoule (MJ) of electricity generated (g CO2e MJ⁻¹). The figures presented in Table 8.1 are approximate.

Table 8.1

source of energycarbon footprint / g CO2e MJ⁻¹
oil1000
coal800
gas500
hydroelectric25
bioethanol12
wind12

Suggest why the carbon footprint in Table 8.1 is measured in terms of an equivalent mass of carbon dioxide. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Suggest why the carbon footprint in Table 8.1 is measured in terms of an equivalent mass of carbon dioxide. [2] [INFERRED: no official key]

1. Several different greenhouse gases are released, and each one traps a different amount of heat per unit mass, that is, each has a different global warming potential, so their masses cannot simply be added together or compared directly.

2. Converting every gas into the mass of carbon dioxide that would have the same warming effect puts them all into one common unit, so the total effect of a mixture of gases can be added up and a valid comparison can be made between different energy sources.

(d) Bioethanol, oil, coal and gas all release large amounts of carbon dioxide during combustion to generate electricity. However, bioethanol has a much lower carbon footprint than oil, coal and gas.

Explain why bioethanol has a much lower carbon footprint than oil, coal and gas. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) Explain why bioethanol has a much lower carbon footprint than oil, coal and gas. [2] [INFERRED: no official key]

1. Bioethanol is made from crop plants that photosynthesise as they grow, taking carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere. The carbon dioxide released when the bioethanol is burned is therefore carbon that was removed from the atmosphere only months or years earlier, and it is taken up again by the next crop, so there is little or no net addition of CO2 to the atmosphere and the fuel is close to carbon neutral.

2. Oil, coal and gas are fossil fuels containing carbon that was fixed millions of years ago and has been locked out of the carbon cycle ever since, so burning them adds carbon dioxide to the atmosphere that is not re-absorbed, giving a large net increase.

3. Two prelim schemes protect this argument in both directions and reject "burning of biofuel releases a large net amount of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, since biofuel is supposed to be carbon neutral" and reject "biofuels make a large contribution to worsening global warming". The permitted criticism of bioethanol is the carbon debt from harvesting, processing and transport, never the combustion.

(e) At the point of generating electricity, no carbon dioxide is released from hydroelectric power stations or wind turbines. State two reasons why wind power and hydroelectric power have carbon footprints that are greater than zero. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (e)

(e) State two reasons why wind power and hydroelectric power have carbon footprints that are greater than zero. [2] [INFERRED: no official key]

1. Carbon dioxide is released during the manufacture of the turbines, generators and dam, because mining and processing the raw materials and making the steel and concrete use energy from fossil fuels.

2. Carbon dioxide is released during construction, transport, installation, maintenance and eventual decommissioning of the equipment, which all use fossil-fuelled machinery and vehicles.

3. Also accept: flooding land to make a hydroelectric reservoir drowns vegetation which then decomposes anaerobically, releasing methane, and destroys forest that had been acting as a carbon sink.

4. The bar chart alone cannot answer this part. Every mark here comes from upstream life-cycle stages, not from generation.

(f) A student writes that coal has the highest carbon footprint of any fossil fuel, because for a given amount of energy released coal produces more carbon dioxide than oil or natural gas. With reference to Table 8.1, evaluate this student's statement. [3]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (f)

(f) With reference to Table 8.1, evaluate the student's claim that coal has the highest carbon footprint of any fossil fuel. [3] [CONSTRUCTED, no real paper question exists for this outcome. The two published rankings and the reject line it is built on are both real: the school's Fig. 2.12 and 9477 Specimen P2 Q8 Table 8.1]

1. The statement does not agree with Table 8.1. In the table oil has the highest carbon footprint at 1000 g CO2e MJ⁻¹, above coal at 800 g CO2e MJ⁻¹ and gas at 500 g CO2e MJ⁻¹, so on this measure oil, not coal, is the highest of the three.

2. The student's reasoning is about a different quantity. The claim that coal produces the most carbon dioxide for a given amount of energy released is about direct emissions at combustion only, on which coal genuinely is the highest of the three fossil fuels. Table 8.1 is a life-cycle figure, calculated over the entire life of the device and expressed per megajoule of electricity generated, so it also counts extraction, refining, transport and construction, and life-cycle accounting can reorder the fuels.

3. Both figures are published and neither is wrong, so the answer is to rank from the table supplied. LO (d) asks only for relative differences, so quote the table's own values and its own units and do not substitute a memorised ranking. Reciting a per-kWh ranking over a per-MJ table is the trap this part exists to catch.

Question 2 [11 marks]

Trees remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and store this carbon in their biomass in the long term. This long-term storage of carbon is called carbon sequestration.

(a) The carbon sequestered in a tree is not in the form of carbon dioxide. Identify three biomolecules in which carbon may be sequestered in a tree. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Identify three biomolecules in which carbon may be sequestered in a tree. [3] [INFERRED: no official key]

1. Cellulose, in the cell walls.

2. Lignin, in the walls of xylem vessels and fibres, that is, wood.

3. Starch, stored in amyloplasts.

4. Also accept protein, lipid, sucrose or glucose. Saying that the carbon is stored in biomass earns nothing, because the question has already told you it is stored in biomass and is asking which molecules.

(b) Singapore has a high density of urban trees and plants, earning it the description 'garden city'. It also has a busy road network. The rain tree, Samanea saman, is the commonest urban tree species in Singapore. Table 2.1 shows the number of rain trees located along roads and in parks in Singapore and the rate at which the trees sequester carbon in tonnes per year. One tonne is equivalent to 1000 kg.

Table 2.1

locationnumber of rain treesrate of carbon sequestration / tonnes year⁻¹
roads26 226487
parks2 35644

For the rain trees located along roads and in parks in Singapore, calculate the mean mass of carbon sequestered by a single rain tree in one year. Show your working and give your answer in kilograms (kg) to three significant figures. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Calculate the mean mass of carbon sequestered by a single rain tree in one year, in kg to three significant figures. [2] [INFERRED: no official key]

1. Total number of trees = 26 226 + 2 356 = 28 582. Total carbon sequestered = 487 + 44 = 531 tonnes = 531 × 1000 = 531 000 kg.

2. Mean mass per tree = 531 000 ÷ 28 582 = 18.578. = 18.6 kg to 3 s.f.

3. A prelim scheme on the same node records the presentation rules that decide these marks: max 1 mark if no headings at all, and the recorded common errors are not writing any headings or formulas and giving the final answer to 2 s.f. where 3 s.f. was asked. Write a heading, then the formula, then the working, then the unit, then the stated significant figures.

(c) In total, Singapore's urban trees sequester 3872 tonnes of the element carbon per year. This helps offset carbon dioxide emissions from human activities like burning fossil fuels in the engines of cars. There are about 600 000 cars in Singapore. Each car is estimated to emit 4.04 tonnes of carbon dioxide per year. 27% of the mass of carbon dioxide is carbon.

Use the data provided to calculate the percentage of the element carbon released into the atmosphere by cars in Singapore that is offset by the urban trees. Show your working. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Calculate the percentage of the element carbon released by cars in Singapore that is offset by the urban trees. [3] [INFERRED: no official key]

1. Total carbon dioxide emitted by cars = 600 000 × 4.04 = 2 424 000 tonnes year⁻¹.

2. Mass of carbon in this = 2 424 000 × 27/100 = 654 480 tonnes year⁻¹.

3. Percentage offset = 3872 ÷ 654 480 × 100 = 0.5916 = 0.59%, accept 0.6%.

(d) With reference to your answer to (c) and any other relevant aspects, comment on the benefits to the environment of planting urban trees in Singapore. [3]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) With reference to your answer to (c) and any other relevant aspects, comment on the benefits to the environment of planting urban trees in Singapore. [3] [INFERRED: no official key]

1. The stance. In terms of carbon the benefit is very small: the urban trees offset only about 0.59%, which is less than 1%, of the carbon released by cars alone, and cars are only one of many sources of emissions, so planting urban trees cannot by itself mitigate Singapore's contribution to climate change and reducing emissions at source matters far more.

2. The qualification that bounds the stance. The calculation understates the value of the trees, because it counts only the carbon fixed in one year while the carbon remains locked in the wood for the whole life of the tree.

3. Other environmental benefits. Trees take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen in photosynthesis; they lower air temperature by shading surfaces and by evaporative cooling from transpiration, reducing the urban heat island effect and so cutting the energy, and the emissions, used for air conditioning; their leaves trap particulates and absorb pollutant gases, improving air quality; they provide habitats and food for insects, birds and other animals, increasing biodiversity; and their roots bind the soil and intercept rainfall, reducing soil erosion, surface run-off and flooding.

4. A prelim scheme on an equivalent evaluate question states that candidates must take an explicit stance and substantiate it with relevant data, and that weaker responses included contradictory data in an attempt to discuss both sides of the argument, but this would not satisfy the requirements of the question. Saying that trees are good for the environment has not answered this part.

Question 3 [5 marks]

(a) There are many greenhouse gases other than carbon dioxide. The overall contribution to global warming of emissions of any greenhouse gas can be calculated using the 100-year global warming potential (GWP). This is specific to each greenhouse gas. Multiplying the mass of greenhouse gas released by its 100-year GWP gives the mass of carbon dioxide that, over a 100-year period, would have the same contribution to global warming.

equivalent mass of carbon dioxide = mass of greenhouse gas released × 100-year GWP

The table shows the masses of five different greenhouse gases released in the UK in 2021, together with their 100-year GWPs.

greenhouse gasmass of gas released / tonnes100-year GWP
carbon dioxide (CO2)3.4 × 10⁸1
methane (CH4)2.0 × 10⁶28
nitrous oxide (N2O)7.2 × 10⁴265
sulfur hexafluoride (SF6)1.8 × 10¹23 500
nitrogen trifluoride (NF3)2.1 × 10⁻²16 100

Which statement correctly describes the effect over a 100-year period of the emission of greenhouse gases in the UK in 2021?

AOf the gases listed in the table, methane was the greenhouse gas responsible for the greatest contribution to global warming.
BSulfur hexafluoride is the most potent of the listed greenhouse gases but contributed to global warming by less than 0.1% of the contribution of carbon dioxide.
CThe contribution of nitrous oxide emissions to global warming was just over one third of the contribution from methane emissions.
DThe contribution to global warming of 18 tonnes of sulfur hexafluoride emissions was equivalent to a little over 27 tonnes of nitrogen trifluoride emissions.

[1]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Which statement correctly describes the effect over a 100-year period of the emission of greenhouse gases in the UK in 2021? [1] [INFERRED: no official key]

1. C

(b) Explain your answer to (a), taking each of the four statements in turn. [4]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Explain your answer, taking each of the four statements in turn. [4] [INFERRED: no official key]

1. Work out the CO2 equivalent for every gas first. CO2 = 3.4 × 10⁸ × 1 = 3.4 × 10⁸ tonnes. CH4 = 2.0 × 10⁶ × 28 = 5.6 × 10⁷ tonnes. N2O = 7.2 × 10⁴ × 265 = 1.91 × 10⁷ tonnes. SF6 = 1.8 × 10¹ × 23 500 = 4.23 × 10⁵ tonnes. NF3 = 2.1 × 10⁻² × 16 100 = 3.4 × 10² tonnes.

2. C is correct. 1.91 × 10⁷ ÷ 5.6 × 10⁷ = 0.341, which is just over one third, since one third is 0.333.

3. A is wrong, because carbon dioxide at 3.4 × 10⁸ contributes far more than methane at 5.6 × 10⁷. A very large mass at a GWP of 1 beats a small mass at a GWP of 28.

4. B is wrong. SF6 does have the highest GWP of the five, but 4.23 × 10⁵ ÷ 3.4 × 10⁸ × 100 = 0.124%, which is more than 0.1%, not less.

5. D is wrong. 4.23 × 10⁵ ÷ 16 100 = 26.3 tonnes of NF3, which is a little under 27 tonnes, not a little over.

6. Note the GWP values the paper supplies: methane 28 and nitrous oxide 265, which are AR5 values. The school teaches methane 25 and nitrous oxide 298, which are AR4 values. Both are published and neither is wrong. A candidate who substitutes a memorised 25 into a table that says 28 gets the arithmetic wrong. Memorise only the shape, that methane is roughly 25 to 30 times as potent as CO2 over a century.

Question 4 [11 marks]

In plants, carbon dioxide (CO2) and water (H2O) are the products of cellular respiration while they are the reactants in photosynthesis. Tropical rain forests are estimated to be responsible for approximately 20% of global photosynthesis, yet the consumption of large amounts of CO2 by living trees is thought to make little or no net contribution to reduction of global warming.

Explain how photosynthesis and cellular respiration are related to the climate and discuss the contributing factors that continue to bring about global warming even with large amounts of CO2 being consumed by trees in the tropical rainforests. [11]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer

Explain how photosynthesis and cellular respiration are related to the climate and discuss the contributing factors that continue to bring about global warming even with large amounts of CO2 being consumed by trees in the tropical rainforests. [11]

1. Greenhouse gases (GHGs) like CO2 and CH4 trap and absorb heat at the Earth's surface, keeping the Earth warm.

2. Ref. to uptake of atmospheric CO2 by photosynthetic organisms.

3. Ref. to sugar molecule formation in the Calvin cycle.

4. Heterotrophs consume plants to obtain the energy trapped.

5. Heterotrophs break down sugars or other forms of respiratory substrates.

6. Ref. to CO2 being produced during link reaction and Krebs cycle.

7. Ref. to the idea of anthropogenic factors, being man-made or actions of humans.

8. Deforestation leads to the cessation of CO2 absorption.

9. Burning of fossil fuels due to increase in global demand for energy.

10. Ref. to how agriculture, rice cultivation, landfill waste, food choices or increase in the consumption of meat contribute to global warming.

11. Leading to increased livestock farming or domestication of animals, ideal conditions for bacteria to decompose organic material, waste decomposing in absence of O2, or enteric fermentation of ruminant animals.

12. Ref. to drastic increase in amount of CO2 and CH4 emissions.

13. QWC: Scientific argumentation exemplified by linking coherently photosynthesis and cellular respiration to the climate as well as how causal factors bring about global warming.

Sources & concepts

Source: School (HCI) Prelim 2018 P3 Q5b, stem and full mark scheme verbatim, at its real 11 marks. This is one of six photosynthesis or respiration crossover essays among the 17 essay-scale Book 8 stems in the papers, which is the commonest Book 8 essay shape by a distance. Archetype: the full-cycle process question of this drill. It is the carbon cycle run end to end, from fixation through consumption to release, and then thrown out of balance by named human activity. Book 8's essays are Core-Idea-bridged, not chapter revision. Trap: describing the carbon cycle as a diagram instead of naming the specific processes. A scheme elsewhere in this Book is explicit that candidates should name specific processes such as carbon fixation and light-dependent reactions instead of leaving it broadly as photosynthesis, and rejects "photosynthesis" where carbon fixation was wanted. The second trap is answering only the first half and never reaching the question actually asked, which is why the rainforest sink does not cancel the emissions. LOs: (a) in full; reach-back Core Idea 3 photosynthesis LOs (c) to (e) and respiration LOs (f) to (k). Concepts fused: (1) the greenhouse mechanism as the link between a gas and a temperature; (2) photosynthetic fixation of atmospheric CO2; (3) the Calvin cycle as the specific fixing process; (4) transfer of fixed carbon to heterotrophs; (5) oxidative decarboxylation in the link reaction and Krebs cycle as the specific releasing process; (6) natural balance of the cycle; (7) deforestation as sink removal; (8) fossil fuel combustion as release of long-buried carbon; (9) anaerobic methanogenesis across paddies, landfill and rumen; (10) why a large sink still leaves a net rise.

Question 5 [10 marks]

(a) A newspaper article on forest loss contains the quote "That's worrisome because those regions store the largest chunks of carbon in ecosystems across the globe." Define the role of forests in storing carbon and explain briefly how they are able to do this. [4]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Define the role of forests in storing carbon and explain briefly how they are able to do this. [4] (Any 4)

1. They act as carbon sinks.

2. A carbon sink refers to a natural or artificial reservoir that accumulates and stores some carbon-containing chemical compound for an indefinite period.

3. The process by which carbon sinks remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere is known as carbon sequestration.

4. This is done by the removal of carbon dioxide from the air during photosynthesis.

5. And the storage of this carbon dioxide in the form of biomolecules like carbohydrates, proteins and lipids.

(b) Plants have long been regarded as carbon sinks because they take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis. However, when temperatures rise, plants increase their rate of respiration, resulting in increased carbon release. Some research has suggested that this could convert forests from a long-term carbon sink to a carbon source, aggravating climate change.

Outline how a rise in temperature could lead to increased carbon release by plants. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Outline how a rise in temperature could lead to increased carbon release by plants. [3]

1. An increase in temperature leads to increased kinetic energy and hence an increase in effective collision between enzyme and substrate, or in rate of enzyme-substrate complex formation.

2. This leads to an increase in rate of the link reaction and Krebs cycle.

3. More carbon is released in the form of carbon dioxide from oxidative decarboxylation reactions.

4. The consequence the stem is pointing at: because a sink absorbs more carbon than it releases and a source releases more than it stores, a forest whose respiration rate rises faster than its photosynthesis rate flips from sink to source. The same forest can be either, which is why the south-eastern Amazon is now a net carbon source.

(c) Termites are a group of insects that consume a wide variety of plant material in the form of wood and leaf litter. They are able to break down cellulose into hexose and pentose oligomers due to the presence of symbiotic cellulolytic bacteria which produce a variety of cellulases. Termites are also known to produce methane as a by-product in the process of breaking down cellulose. The global methane emission from this source is estimated to be 20 million tonnes each year.

Explain how termites can worsen the effects of climate change as global temperature increases. [3]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Explain how termites can worsen the effects of climate change as global temperature increases. [3]

1. Increasing temperature increases metabolism or reproduction rate in termites, resulting in a larger termite population.

2. Increased temperature increases enzymatic activity in bacteria in termites, resulting in a faster methane production.

3. Increase in methane production causes an increased greenhouse effect, trapping more heat in the atmosphere.

4. This causes a further increase in temperature, resulting in a positive feedback loop.

Sources & concepts

Source: SRJC Prelim 2017 P3 Q1c, stem and key verbatim (a), with the article quote kept and the surrounding comprehension passage dropped so the part stands alone; ACJC Prelim 2018 P3 Q3a, stem and all three marking points verbatim (b), with marking point 4 added here to name the sink-to-source flip the stem sets up; RI Prelim 2024 P3 Q2(c), stem and all four marking points verbatim (c). Archetype: definition, then a mechanism chain run through enzyme kinetics, then the same enzyme argument transferred to an unfamiliar organism and closed with a feedback classification. Recall is genuinely common on this concept heading at 31%, the only place in Book 8 where it is. Trap: defining a carbon sink by the size of its store rather than by the net direction of carbon movement; giving "respiration increases" for (b) without naming the link reaction, Krebs cycle or oxidative decarboxylation, when a scheme in this Book rejects umbrella process names; and stopping (c) at "termites make methane" without the population term, the bacterial enzyme term or the loop. LOs: (a) in (b) and (c); (c) carbon sinks and sequestration in (a); reach-back Core Idea 1 LO (q) enzymes and temperature, and Core Idea 3 respiration LOs (f) to (k). Concepts fused: (1) carbon sink defined by net direction; (2) sequestration as the removal process; (3) fixation into named biomolecule classes; (4) kinetic energy, effective collisions and enzyme-substrate complex formation; (5) the link reaction and Krebs cycle as the CO2-releasing steps; (6) oxidative decarboxylation; (7) sink-to-source inversion; (8) symbiotic cellulase digestion; (9) methanogenesis as a by-product of anaerobic cellulose breakdown; (10) positive feedback classification.

Question 6 [7 marks]

(a) The emission of greenhouse gases such as CO2 and CH4 have different impacts on global warming depending on their concentration in the atmosphere, their atmospheric lifetime and their global warming potential (GWP). Which row correctly best describes the characteristics of these greenhouse gases?

CO2CH4
Ahigher GWPlower GWP
Bfrom anthropogenic activities such as decomposition of waste at landfillsfrom anthropogenic activities such as manure management of livestock
Cfrom natural processes such as soil respirationfrom natural processes such as ruminant digestion
Dshorter atmospheric lifetimelonger atmospheric lifetime

[1]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Which row correctly best describes the characteristics of CO2 and CH4? [1]

1. C, CO2 from natural processes such as soil respiration, and CH4 from natural processes such as ruminant digestion.

(b) Explain your answer to (a), taking each of the other three rows in turn and stating why it is wrong. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Explain your answer, taking each of the other three rows in turn. [3]

1. Why C is right. Soil respiration by decomposers and roots is the major natural source of carbon dioxide, and methanogenic archaea in the rumen of cattle and other ruminants are a major natural source of methane.

2. Reject A, because methane has a far higher global warming potential than carbon dioxide per unit mass, not lower.

3. Reject B, because decomposition of waste at landfills is anaerobic and releases methane, not carbon dioxide.

4. Reject D, because carbon dioxide persists in the atmosphere for very much longer than methane, which is oxidised within about a decade.

5. Row B is the useful one to think through, because the four anthropogenic methane sources named in this Book, enteric fermentation, manure management, rice paddies and landfill, are all the same mechanism: oxygen-poor conditions in which bacteria decompose organic material to produce CH4. Learn them as one anaerobic mechanism and you can generate the list rather than recall it.

(c) Fig. 11.1 shows the annual change in atmospheric methane concentrations at Baring Head, New Zealand between 1990 and 2022. The dashed line shows the change in atmospheric methane concentration from year to year.

With reference to Fig. 11.1, deduce how the change in atmospheric methane concentration between 2004 and 2022 could affect the temperatures at Baring Head during this period. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) With reference to Fig. 11.1, deduce how the change in atmospheric methane concentration between 2004 and 2022 could affect the temperatures at Baring Head during this period. [2]

1. As the rate of change of methane increased from 2004 to 2022, temperatures would have increased at a more drastic rate at Baring Head.

2. This is because methane is a greenhouse gas that traps heat in the atmosphere.

3. Read the y-axis carefully. It is the annual change in concentration, not the concentration, so a rising curve means methane is accumulating faster each year, and even the minimum around 2003 to 2004 is positive, meaning methane never stopped rising.

(d) Carbon dioxide is similar to methane with respect to its negative impact in the atmosphere and environment. Name one other naturally-occurring gas in the atmosphere that could have the same negative impact resulting in climate change. [1]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) Name one other naturally-occurring gas in the atmosphere that could have the same negative impact resulting in climate change. [1]

1. Water vapour, and the scheme rejects "water" and "H2O".

2. Nitrous oxide, and the scheme rejects the formula "N2O" on its own.

3. Ozone, and the scheme rejects "O3" on its own.

4. Reject chlorofluorocarbon, because it is not naturally occurring. Accept hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), perfluorocarbons (PFCs), sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) and nitrogen trifluoride (NF3).

(a) Explain how increased meat production contributes to an increase in another greenhouse gas such as carbon dioxide in the environment. [2]

Deforestation occurs to convert land into farmland to raise livestock, and carbon stored by trees is released into the atmosphere as carbon dioxide when trees are burned or through decomposition of the remaining organic matter, or there are fewer trees to take in carbon dioxide from the environment.

2. Farming livestock does not produce as much food per acre as growing crops, or more land used for farming livestock or growing animal feed means less land to grow crops for humans.

Question 8 [10 marks]

The concept of climate change and global warming has been of concern to scientists for many years. One way to collect data about atmospheric concentrations of greenhouse gases in the past is to study samples of ice from ice sheets in Antarctica. Ice samples from deep in the ice sheets were formed hundreds of thousands of years ago, while those near the surface were formed recently. As ice forms, small bubbles of air are trapped in the ice. These air bubbles can be analysed to determine the concentration of carbon dioxide present. It is also possible to use chemical techniques to determine when the air bubbles were trapped. Scientists studying climate change measured carbon dioxide concentrations in air bubbles from ice samples of known age, collected from near the surface. Fig. 11.1 shows the concentration of carbon dioxide measured in air bubbles that were trapped in ice from 1959 to 1990. Direct measurements of atmospheric carbon dioxide from 1948 to 1978 are also shown.

(a) With reference to the information provided, suggest and explain how climate change scientists can estimate atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations 10 000 years ago. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) With reference to the information provided, suggest and explain how climate change scientists can estimate atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations 10 000 years ago. [2]

1. Suggest: Scientists can analyse the concentration of carbon dioxide in air bubbles trapped deeper in the ice sheets 10 000 years ago, as an estimate of the atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations then, and extract ice samples from different depths of the ice sheets and determine the age of the ice samples.

2. Explain: The graph in Fig. 11.1 shows that the concentration of carbon dioxide measured in air bubbles trapped in ice is a good and accurate match with the direct measurements of atmospheric carbon dioxide at the time when the air bubbles were formed, so air bubbles could be regarded as samples of the atmosphere from the time at which they formed, that is, the bubble measurement is a good indicator of atmospheric carbon dioxide levels.

(b) It is possible to estimate past temperatures by analysing the ratio of the hydrogen isotope ¹H to the hydrogen isotope ²H in ice samples. The ratio of ¹H to ²H increases as the temperature increases. Fig. 11.2 shows the ratio of ¹H to ²H in ice samples formed over the last 800 000 years and the corresponding atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations.

Use Fig. 11.2 to comment on changes in temperature over the last 800 000 years. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Use Fig. 11.2 to comment on changes in temperature over the last 800 000 years. [2]

1. Rise and fall of the ratio of ¹H to ²H corresponds with the percentage concentration of carbon dioxide.

2. Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas, so an increased concentration in the atmosphere leads to more heat being trapped, and there is a rise and fall of temperature as the concentration of carbon dioxide changes.

3. The reasoning depends on the sentence the paper gave you, that the ratio of ¹H to ²H increases as the temperature increases, so the upper trace is a temperature proxy and not a temperature measurement.

3. From 1880 to 1933, the global temperatures were lower than the mean, while from 1933 to 2020, the global temperatures were above the mean. Data: from 1880 to 1933, the mean global surface temperature difference fluctuates between -0.38 °C and 0.0 °C, and from 1933 to 2020, temperature increases from 0.0 °C to 0.86 °C.

Question 9 [12 marks]

People make use of chemical energy stored in plants by burning biofuels. Biofuels are fuels that are produced from crop plants grown specifically for this purpose. People also use chemical energy stores from plants that lived millions of years ago by burning coal, which is a fossil fuel.

Discuss the benefits and risks to society of using these two sources of plant chemical energy as fuels. [12]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer

Discuss the benefits and risks to society of using these two sources of plant chemical energy as fuels. [12]

1. Maximum six from benefits and risks of using biofuels. Benefits: BB1a Biofuel is a renewable resource, accept sustainable. BB1b Crop plants utilised for biofuel production cannot be depleted, or can be grown and harvested within months. BB2a Reference to carbon neutrality, or cause less air pollution. BB2b Crop plants absorb atmospheric carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, thus offsetting carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere when biofuels are burned. BB3a Reference to economic independence. BB3b Costs of oil and gas imports can be offset by adoption of biofuels, especially if fuel crops like corn and sugar cane are grown locally. BB4a Reference to cost effectiveness, or easier and cheaper sources for biofuels. BB4b Reference to wide variety of photosynthetic organisms such as crop plants and microalgae.

2. Risks of biofuels: BR1a Some agricultural land used for food crop production is converted for fuel crop production. BR1b Reference to impact on food supply chain and increase in food prices. BR2a Monoculture of fuel crop, for example corn, reduces plant genetic diversity, or requires the application of fertilisers. BR2b Reference to use of fertilisers causing water pollution. AVP: reference to crop failure due to pest or drought affecting supply; high cost of extraction. Reject: biofuels make a large contribution to worsening global warming, since they are supposed to be carbon neutral.

3. Maximum six from benefits and risks of using fossil fuels, awarding global warming under FR2. Benefits: FB1a Fossil fuel is more reliable than renewable energy. FB1b Reference to renewable energy, for example wind or solar power, being limited in efficiency by unfavourable environmental conditions. FB1c Fossil fuel can be stored for an indefinite period of time. FB2a Fossil fuel is abundant or accessible. FB2b Natural gas and oil are typically transported easily via international gas pipeline systems or with tankers. FB3a Fossil fuels have higher energy efficiency than biofuels. FB3b Reference to less fossil fuel needed to provide the same amount of energy, for example gasoline has 50% more energy content than bioethanol.

4. Risks of fossil fuels: FR1a Fossil fuel is a non-renewable or finite resource. FR1b Reference to depletion of oil and natural gas in 50 years and coal in 100 years. FR2a Burning of fossil fuel releases carbon dioxide or greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. Reject: burning of biofuel releases a large net amount of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, since biofuel is supposed to be carbon neutral, so FR2a is not awarded. FR2b Reference to greenhouse gases causing global warming. FR2c Reference to any one effect of greenhouse gas emissions, for example melting of polar ice caps, rising sea levels, stress on fresh water supplies, heat waves, heavy rains, death of coral reefs, migration of fishes and insects, release of greenhouse gases in frozen organic matter. FR3a Natural gas is a combustible material and can cause explosions. FR3b Oil spills cause water pollution.

5. Maximum three from benefits and risks of using both: B1 Combustion of fossil fuels or biofuels generates electricity. B2 Reference to use of electricity in industry or transportation. B3 Reference to burning of both fossil fuels and biofuels being safer than use of nuclear energy to generate electricity. B4 Reference to burning of both being more stable or reliable than wind or solar power to generate electricity; award once for FB1a or B4. B5 Creation of jobs in the agricultural or mining sector, reducing unemployment. R1 Reference to deforestation or clearing of forest for fuel crop production or mining of fossil fuel. R2 Reference to deforestation resulting in loss of carbon sink. R3 Reference to loss of biodiversity.

6. Misconceptions to avoid: carbon dioxide in the atmosphere has direct adverse effects on lung health; biofuels make a large contribution to worsening global warming, since they are supposed to be carbon neutral; burning coal, oil or gas releases uncombusted methane gas into the atmosphere, when methane is a component of natural gas; emissions from burning fuels damage the ozone layer, when it is the CFCs.

7. QWC: Good spread of knowledge communicated without ambiguity in appropriate sections, with discussion of at least one benefit and one risk for each source of plant chemical energy supported with facts.

Sources & concepts

Source: Timed Practice Exercise 2024 P3 Q5b, stem and the entire mark scheme verbatim including every code, every reject line and the misconception list, at its real 12 marks. Archetype: the discuss archetype. Discuss runs at, more than four times Book 3, and with the comment and evaluate parts roughly. This is the largest such part in the papers for LO (d). Trap: the whole scheme is built around one trap, that attacking biofuel combustion is rejected twice by name. The permitted criticism of biofuel is the land competition, the food price effect, the monoculture and the fertiliser pollution, never the CO2 released when it burns. The second trap is writing an unstructured sweep and missing the QWC requirement of at least one benefit and one risk for each of the two fuels. LOs: (d) energy production in full; (a) through the fossil fuel and deforestation risks; a reach-back to genetic diversity and monoculture that Cluster 3 will take further. Concepts fused: (1) renewability as a defined property; (2) carbon neutrality and its true boundary; (3) energy density as a benefit of fossil fuels; (4) reliability and storability against intermittency; (5) land competition between fuel and food crops; (6) monoculture and genetic diversity; (7) fertiliser run-off; (8) finite reserves and depletion timescales; (9) the greenhouse chain from combustion to a named effect; (10) deforestation as sink loss shared by both fuels; (11) taking a stance while bounding it with the counter-argument.
